text: In a 40,000-sample study of forbidden-word constraints, 87.5% of violations were 'priming failures' (naming the word activated it) and 12.5% were 'override failures' from late-layer feed-forward networks; violation probability follows a logistic curve in the model's intrinsic probability of the forbidden token. (low confidence)

Mentioning a topic in the prompt makes the model more likely to mention it even when told to avoid it (the Pink Elephant problem); prompting alone was outperformed by a Llama-2-13B model fine-tuned with Direct Principle Feedback, which matched GPT-4 on the authors' test set. (medium confidence)
Listing banned words in a style prompt is an antipattern: the list itself places the tokens in context and primes them; pair any unavoidable prohibition with a named replacement. (medium confidence)

Circuit analysis suggests sparse middle-layer attention heads amplify forbidden tokens while early layers suppress them, so ironic rebound reflects competing internal representations rather than simple suppression. (low confidence)

Anthropic's prompting docs advise telling Claude what to do instead of what not to do (e.g. replace 'Do not use markdown' with a positive description of the wanted prose format). (medium confidence) (verified as of 2026-09-23)

The backfire is scoped, not universal: a small code-review test found prohibitions matched the positive reframe on discrete actions and underperformed only on judgment calls (2/3 false positives with prohibition vs 0/3 with reframe); earlier inverse-scaling evidence came from classification tasks on older models. (low confidence)

Negation instructions such as 'do not mention X' can paradoxically increase the accessibility of X in LLMs (ironic rebound); rebound appears immediately after negation and worsens with longer or semantic distractor text, while repetition supports suppression. (medium confidence)
